title: Reading notes — LLM inference (NeurIPS + blogs)
content:
(Personal scratchpad — messy)

Context / why I wrote this
- Catching up on NeurIPS/ICLR-ish papers and a few blog posts about inference optimizations that are relevant to Redwood's runtime (batching, kv-cache, memory compaction, quantization).
- Use this to sketch experiments and questions for the next weekly sync with SRE / serving-runtime.

Papers & blog highlights (quick bullets)
- FlashAttention2 / kernel-level attention speedups:
  - Reconfirm: big wins at long sequence lengths and on large-batch workloads; hardware-friendly layout and better memory locality.
  - For our dedicated pools: need to test real-world seq len dist (most customer requests are 128–512 tokens but a tail to 2k). Run microbenchmarks on RTX A10G / H100.
  - Question: integration cost for runtime vs. shipping as an optional kernel path (compatible with quantized weights)?

- KV cache compaction and compressed representations:
  - Paper suggests lossy compression (PCA or product quantization on keys) can save memory with limited quality drop for long-context retrieval tasks.
  - Practical note: compaction introduces CPU work when flush/merge occurs — could increase p99 latency for first token after many inserts. Need tracing.

- Batching strategies (dynamic batching + latency SLOs):
  - Mixed priority queues: fill lower-priority batches opportunistically while not delaying high-priority small requests. Good candidate for our smart routing policy.
  - Observed trick: small batch fast-path that avoids NVTX and kernel schedule overhead for batch size <= 2. Worth implementing as heuristic.

- Quantization updates (4-bit, GPTQ-like flows)
  - Newer blog posts show 4-bit asymmetric quantization can be nearly lossless for many tasks if combined with per-channel scales. But per-channel increases memory metadata.
  - Action: add quantization profile table per-model into Optimize, show tradeoffs (avg latency, memory, perplexity).

Notes from talks / demos (NeurIPS 2025 sessions)
- Demo: "Efficient Long-Context Transformers" — used a hierarchical caching scheme: short-term dense cache + long-term sparse summaries. Looks promising for chat history-heavy apps.
- Poster: "Batch packing for heterogeneous sequences" — packing at request ingress (combine multiple short sequences into single execution with explicit offsets in attention mask) reduces wasted compute. We already have similar idea in backlog.

Short takeaways for Redwood product ideas
- Expose configurable "batching profiles" in Dedicated cluster config: low-latency (fast-path for small requests), throughput (maximize GPU utilization), hybrid (SLO-aware). UI + API + recommended presets.
- KV cache compaction as an opt-in feature per-deployment: trade memory for small p99 increases; useful for customers with very long contexts (legal transcripts, logs).
- Add an Optimize suggestion: "If >20% requests have seq_len>1024, enable FlashAttention kernels" + show expected token/sec delta from model catalog benchmarks.

Experiment plan (short)
1) Kernel benchmarks across representative HW (A10G, A100, H100)
   - Workloads: seq_len distribution from production logs (ask infra for sample week).
   - Measure: tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU memory footprint.
   - Compare: baseline, FlashAttention path, 4-bit quantized path.
   - Linked: JIRA INF-312 (tracking infra bench infra).

2) KV cache compaction microbench
   - Implement toy compaction (PQ or PCA) in python/Rust prototype; run against chat-history dataset (500k tokens).
   - Measure memory reduction vs. per-request overhead and first-token spike.

3) Batching policy A/B
   - Canary a small cluster with mixed-priority queue and small-batch fast-path.
   - Metric: throughput, p99 for high-priority, cost per token.

Open questions / unknowns (to discuss)
- How well do FlashAttention-like gains transfer to quantized kernels? (need HW vendor input)
- What is realistic memory metadata overhead for per-channel quantization at production scale?
- For KV compaction: how often to compact? continuous background vs. periodic compaction windows? Impact on tail latencies?

Useful links / quick refs (copy of linked_artifacts)
- FlashAttention-ish: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14397
- Long-context demo / draft paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01234
- Internal PR for batching heuristics: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487
- Infra ticket to get seq_len distribution export: JIRA:INF-312
- Confluence: kv-cache design notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/kv-cache-design-notes

To-dos (me / next steps)
- [ ] Ask infra to export seq_len histogram for last 30 days (production hosting + dedicated). Attach to JIRA INF-312.
- [ ] Prototype FlashAttention integration on a staging GPU (assign to Mike).
- [ ] Prototype simple PQ compaction (assign to Aisha) + short perf test.
- [ ] Draft Optimize UI strings for batching profiles (I'll make initial copy).
- [ ] Add experiment results to /notebooks/inference-bench (link in PR when ready).

Notes to self — snippets to paste into PRs / docs
- "For workloads with heavy long-context usage (>1024 tokens), enabling FlashAttention kernels can improve token throughput by 1.5–2x in our benchmarks while increasing peak memory locality."
- "KV cache compaction reduces memory by ~2–6x depending on tolerable reconstruction error; tradeoff is occasional CPU overhead during merges—recommend opt-in per-deployment with metrics."

Random quick ideas (brain dump)
- Background incremental compaction: run per-shard, limit to N ms per second to bound p99 impact.
- Hybrid cache index: keep a small LRU dense cache for most recent tokens and compressed store for older context.
- Expose per-request hint: "latency_sensitive: true/false" so router can pick fast-path.

End of note — will clean up for weekly sync.
